title: Best Pair of Lookout Points
statement:
A trail has lookout points at miles 0, 1, 2, …. The view at point i is worth values[i]. If you visit two points i < j, you enjoy both views but lose one unit for every mile between them, so the pair scores

values[i] + values[j] − (j − i).

Return the highest score any pair of two different points can reach.

examples.why: Points 0 and 2: 5 + 4 − 2 = 7. Neighbours 0 and 1 lose only 1 mile but score just 5.
The two best views, 10 and 9, are 5 miles apart and score 14. The neighbours 9 and 8 score 16.
With two points there is one pair: 3 + 3 − 1.

hints: Split the score into a part that depends only on i and a part that depends only on j.
values[i] + values[j] − (j − i) = (values[i] + i) + (values[j] − j). For a fixed j, which i is best?
Walk j left to right and keep the largest values[i] + i seen so far. Each j scores that maximum plus values[j] − j.

explain.intuition:
The distance term ties i and j together, which suggests checking every pair. But it splits cleanly: values[i] + values[j] − j + i = (values[i] + i) + (values[j] − j). The left point contributes values[i] + i and the right point contributes values[j] − j, independently.

So for each right point j the best partner is simply the earlier point with the largest values[i] + i. Keep that running maximum while you walk the array, and the whole search becomes one pass. It is the same move as "best time to buy and sell": keep the best start seen so far and try every end.
steps: For j from 1 to n − 1: update best = max(best, bestLeft + values[j] − j).
Then update bestLeft = max(bestLeft, values[j] + j), so j can be a left point for later indices.
pitfalls: Picking the two largest values. The second example shows the distance can outweigh a bigger view.
Updating bestLeft with values[j] + j before scoring j. Then j can pair with itself.
Starting best at 0. Every score is at least 1 here, but the habit breaks when values can be small or negative.

solutions.title: Every pair
solutions.idea: Score every pair i < j and keep the best.

solutions.title: Running best left point
solutions.idea: The score splits into (values[i] + i) + (values[j] − j). Keep the best left part seen so far and try each j as the right point.

followups: Pick three points i < j < k with score values[i] + values[j] + values[k] − (k − i). How many running values do you need?
Return the pair of indices too; on ties, the pair with the smallest i.
